newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia gives Khmer Rouge defectors top army posts.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia gives Khmer Rouge defectors top army posts.

text.p: Cambodia on Friday named more than 200 defectors from the Khmer Rouge, the Maoists who killed more than a million people during their 1970s reign of terror, to senior army posts.

Co-Ministers of Defence Tea Banh and Tea Chamrath said 19 of their former foes, part of a wave of recent Khmer Rouge defections, would become generals, including three as advisers to the government. More than 200 would become colonels.
A total of 18,345 former rebels will form eight new divisions and two regiments, the two ministers said.
"We have to forget the past. If we carry on fighting, how many people more are going to die?" Tea Banh said at a news conference.

He and Tea Chamrath said it was time to erase the memory of the Khmer Rouge and their 1975-1979 "killing fields" rule of radical agrarian reform during which more than a million Cambodians died through torture, disease, starvation or overwork.
"Today is an historic day as the government decides to officially recognise the Khmer Rouge defectors and give them official posts," Tea Banh said.
Four men close to the Khmer Rouge's most infamous commanders become major (two-star) generals.

They are Ny Korn, brother of top Khmer Rouge hardliner Son Sen; Ei Chien, former commander of northwestern Pailin; Ta Muth, son-in-law of the one-legged northern rebel commander Ta Mok; and Sam Bith, a former deputy to Ta Mok.
Ei Chien will also become governor of the newly partitioned town of Pailin, his former rebel base, while the other three two-star generals will become advisers to the Ministry of Defence.
"They (the three advisers) are very important people for the government to work with," said Tea Banh.
The former northwest rebel bases of Samlaut, Kom Rieng, Sampou Luon, Ta Sanh and Veal Veng will become provincial districts under government control.

Tea Banh said the posts had been approved by co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who had been at odds over recruitment of rebels, with each leader seeking to win defectors over to his side.
Ieng Sary, the leader who broke the Khmer Rouge apart with the defection of his 4,000 troops in August, will not get an army post.
"Ieng Sary is an old, experienced politician, and the government is only making arrangements for the army," Tea Banh said.
The Khmer Rouge, who reneged on a 1991 peace pact, have been fighting the government since U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993 but hardcore rebels are believed now to number less than 2,000.
